newsitem.title: USA: Defense want "Unabomber" trial to be in Sacramento.
newsitem.headline: Defense want "Unabomber" trial to be in Sacramento.

text.p: Attorneys for Unabomber suspect Theodore Kaczynski said Friday they did not plan to ask the court to move the high-profile trial out of Sacramento.
Kaczynski, a former mathematics professor, is accused of being the shadowy Unabomber, who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995.
He is due to go on trial in Sacramento in November.
Last week, federal prosecutors said they would seek the death penalty if he were convicted.
"We would like to try it here if we can," lead defence attorney Quin Denvir told U.S. District Judge Garland Burrell, the judge in charge of the case.
Some observers thought the defence would seek a change of venue because of pretrial publicity in Sacramento, where Kaczynski has been charged with four bomb attacks, two of them fatal.
Burrell did not rule Friday on a motion by the defence to suppress evidence seized from Kaczynski's remote Montana cabin.
Kaczynksi made a rare appearance in court for the hearing. He wore a brown jacket, black slacks, and a white open-collared shirt.
He appeared to be following the arguments closely during the hearing, which lasted more than two hours. When court was adjourned, he smiled and shook hands with his lawyers.
Kaczynski, arrested in Montana a year ago, has pleaded not guilty to Sacramento charges accusing him of the four bomb attacks.

The defence team Friday asked Burrell to throw out all of the evidence seized by the FBI at the cabin. The defence alleged that the search was illegal because the FBI's affidavit supporting its request for a search warrant contained misleading information.

Investigators found handwritten and handprinted documents at Kaczynski's cabin, written in English, Spanish and numeric code, according to court documents. Prosecutors said Kaczynski's handwritten diary contained phrases such as "I mailed that bomb" or "I sent that bomb."

According to news reports, investigators also found at the cabin bomb components, an original copy of the Unabomber's rambling, 35,000-word anti-technology manifesto sent to newspapers in 1995 and a typewriter used to type it.
At the end of Friday's hearing, Judge Burrell said he would review all the court filings and issue a written ruling later on whether to suppress the cabin evidence.
"I will rule as soon as I can," Burrell said. "It will take some time."
